metadata.research_goal: Define evidence-based tennis teaching progressions from beginner to advanced, including red-orange-green-yellow ball concepts, adult and youth pathways, skill gates, assessments, safe promotion or hold rules, lesson structures, competition entry, and backend records needed for planning.

source_refs.title: Transitioning from Red to Orange to Green
Epidemiology of Injuries in Tennis Players
relevance: shoulder, elbow, wrist, trunk, and lower-limb injury risk

source_refs.title: Epidemiology of Tennis-Related Injuries Among Competitive Youth Tennis Players

key_concepts.concept: Beginner tennis should start with serve, rally, and score, not isolated perfect strokes.
key_concepts.summary: The first backend progression gate is functional play: can the player start points, sustain a simple rally, understand boundaries and scoring, and finish a short game without pain or confusion.
key_concepts.backend_use: Prioritize play tasks before high-detail stroke diagnostics in beginner plans.

key_concepts.concept: Red, orange, and green balls are developmental tools, not lesser versions of tennis.
key_concepts.summary: Lower-compression balls, smaller courts, and shorter rackets create reachable contact heights, longer decision time, and more successful rallies, which lets technical and tactical learning happen together.
key_concepts.backend_use: Store ball stage as a planning input, not only as an age label.

key_concepts.concept: Promotion should be based on readiness, confidence, control, and safety, not age alone.
key_concepts.summary: Age bands guide court and ball choice, but backend promotion should require observed skill gates: consistent contact, rally tolerance, directional control, movement quality, scoring competence, and stable pain response.
key_concepts.backend_use: Implement promotion rules with pass, hold, and temporary-regression outcomes.

key_concepts.concept: Red ball stage emphasizes immediate rally success, simple movement, and cooperative-to-competitive play.
key_concepts.summary: Red ball work should teach ready position, contact in front, simple forehand/backhand swings, starter serves, return awareness, recovery to a balanced position, and small-court tactics.
key_concepts.backend_use: Use red stage for children and for some adult beginners who need slower balls to establish control.

key_concepts.concept: Orange ball stage bridges small-court control into longer movement and intentional direction.
key_concepts.summary: The court is larger, the ball moves faster than red, and lessons should add recovery, depth targets, basic topspin, serve direction, return positioning, and simple open-space tactics.
key_concepts.backend_use: Create orange lessons around rally plus decision tasks, not only harder feeding.

key_concepts.concept: Green ball stage prepares players for full-court yellow-ball tennis while preserving learnable bounce and speed.
key_concepts.summary: Green stage should test full-court coverage, higher rally tolerance, depth control, serve and return reliability, transition decisions, and first competition habits before yellow ball volume rises.
key_concepts.backend_use: Treat green as the main readiness check before regular yellow-ball match schedules.

key_concepts.concept: Yellow ball progression should be earned through full-court control and load tolerance.
key_concepts.summary: Yellow-ball play demands faster decisions, higher bounce management, larger court recovery, and greater impact loads; premature transition can reduce rally quality and raise frustration or load risk.
key_concepts.backend_use: Require green-stage technical, tactical, and physical gates before defaulting a youth plan to yellow ball.

key_concepts.concept: Adults can use orange or green balls without changing the goal of adult tennis.
key_concepts.summary: Slower balls help adults rally earlier, reduce rushed swings, and make serve-return-score lessons possible before full-speed ball reading is reliable.
key_concepts.backend_use: Give adult beginner plans a ball-speed field with orange, green, or yellow defaults by assessment.

key_concepts.concept: Youth progression should develop athletic, cognitive, social, and emotional competencies alongside tennis skills.
key_concepts.summary: A youth player who hits better but cannot cooperate, self-regulate, solve simple tactical problems, or move safely is not ready for more demanding tennis environments.
key_concepts.backend_use: Assessment records should include confidence, character, connection, competence, and creativity signals.

key_concepts.concept: Pre-teen tennis development should preserve broad physical literacy.
key_concepts.summary: Running, jumping, throwing, catching, balance, rhythm, and multi-direction movement support later tennis skill and reduce the need for narrow early specialization.
key_concepts.backend_use: Beginner and youth plans should include non-racket athletic tasks, not only court feeding.

key_concepts.concept: Every promotion decision needs a technical, tactical, and physical-readiness gate.
key_concepts.summary: A player may have enough stroke control but lack recovery movement, scoring understanding, or pain tolerance; backend rules should avoid promoting on one dimension alone.
key_concepts.backend_use: Create composite readiness scores for contact, decision, movement, and load response.

key_concepts.concept: Holding a player at a level is a developmental decision, not failure.
key_concepts.summary: A hold is appropriate when promotion causes rally breakdown, unsafe movement, avoidant tactics, loss of confidence, repeated pain flags, or poor competition behavior.
key_concepts.backend_use: Store hold reasons so the next plan targets the actual blocker.

key_concepts.concept: Assessments should be task-based and repeatable.
key_concepts.summary: Useful assessments include rally counts, serve-in percentages, return-in percentages, depth target success, directional target success, recovery observation, scoring tasks, and post-session pain response.
key_concepts.backend_use: Avoid subjective level upgrades without recorded task outcomes.

key_concepts.concept: Competition should enter early as low-stakes play before ranking-focused events.
key_concepts.summary: Team challenges, round robins, short formats, and modified scoring let players learn scoring, warm-up, etiquette, recovery between points, and emotional regulation without over-weighting win-loss outcomes.
key_concepts.backend_use: Create competition entry records that escalate format length and consequence gradually.

key_concepts.concept: Beginner tactics should be simple, visible, and tied to ball control.
key_concepts.summary: The first tactical layer is send the ball over, recover, find space, keep the ball away from the opponent, and choose safer targets; complex pattern language should wait.
key_concepts.backend_use: Beginner lesson generation should not assign advanced pattern goals before rally gates are met.

key_concepts.concept: Intermediate progression is the point where stroke technique becomes pattern reliability.
key_concepts.summary: Intermediate players need crosscourt tolerance, depth and height control, serve plus-one habits, return plus-one habits, transition options, and controlled change of direction under moderate pressure.
key_concepts.backend_use: Generate intermediate blocks around repeatable tactical patterns with technical constraints.

key_concepts.concept: Advanced progression is opponent-, surface-, score-, and schedule-specific.
key_concepts.summary: Advanced players should refine weapons, protect liabilities, build serve-return-plus-one packages, adapt to surfaces, manage tournament density, and rehearse score-state decisions.
key_concepts.backend_use: Advanced plans should require context fields before prescribing tactical work.

key_concepts.concept: A tennis lesson should cycle through warm-up, live skill, decision task, play application, assessment, and recovery check.
key_concepts.summary: The same lesson skeleton can scale from red ball to advanced: prepare the body, set the technical idea, create a live decision, play points, measure outcomes, and record pain or fatigue response.
key_concepts.backend_use: Use one lesson-template engine with level-specific constraints.

teaching_sequence: short swing from below the ball
contact in front and to the side
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can rally 6-10 cooperative forehands on a red court while keeping balance and contact in front.
technical_models.assessment: Coach records rally count, contact-in-front count, and recovery after each hit.
technical_models.hold_rule: Stay in red if contact is late, swing is mostly across the body, or recovery is consistently absent.

teaching_sequence: show two-handed backhand first for most beginners
turn with both hands on racket
swing low-to-high through a simple target
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can alternate forehand and backhand feeds without changing grip slowly enough to lose readiness.
technical_models.assessment: Ten-ball alternating feed with score for correct side recognition, balanced contact, and in-court result.
technical_models.hold_rule: Hold progression if player runs around every backhand or cannot identify backhand side early.

technical_models.skill_gate: Player starts 7 of 10 points with a legal, in-court serve motion from the appropriate line or court length.
technical_models.assessment: Ten serve attempts tracked for legal start, direction, balance, and pain response.
technical_models.hold_rule: Do not add high-volume serving if toss control, shoulder comfort, or landing balance is unstable.

technical_models.skill_gate: Player returns 6 of 10 controlled beginner serves into the court and recovers for the next ball.
technical_models.assessment: Serve-return-start task with score for readiness, in-court return, and recovery step.
technical_models.hold_rule: Hold if player waits flat-footed, swings too large, or cannot start the rally from return.

technical_models.skill_gate: Player completes simple forehand and backhand volleys into a large target with no backswing.
technical_models.assessment: Ten forehand and ten backhand volleys from close range, scored for contact, racket path, and target area.
technical_models.hold_rule: Hold if player swings like a groundstroke or turns away from the ball.

technical_models.model: Orange-stage groundstroke depth and direction model
teaching_sequence: shape ball over net with margin
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can rally crosscourt on both sides and hit at least half of balls past a mid-court depth marker.
technical_models.assessment: Crosscourt rally or coach-fed target task with depth, direction, and balance scoring.
technical_models.hold_rule: Stay in orange if full-court attempts cause consistent short, late, or off-balance contact.

teaching_sequence: serve and return from regulation positions
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can rally, serve, return, and recover on a full court with green ball without losing contact quality.
technical_models.assessment: Serve-return-rally assessment plus 20-ball groundstroke target test.
technical_models.hold_rule: Delay yellow transition if full-court movement causes rushed swings, poor recovery, or repeated pain response.

technical_models.model: Intermediate forehand as controllable pattern shot
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can rally crosscourt with depth, change height intentionally, and attack a short ball without losing balance.
technical_models.assessment: Crosscourt tolerance, depth ladder, and short-ball attack sequence.
technical_models.hold_rule: Do not add advanced forehand weapon work until neutral forehand error rate is controlled.

technical_models.model: Intermediate backhand with drive, height, and slice option
teaching_sequence: use height and depth to reset
introduce slice for low or defensive balls
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can maintain backhand crosscourt exchanges and choose drive or slice by ball height.
technical_models.assessment: Backhand pattern test with neutral drive, defensive height, and slice response tasks.
technical_models.hold_rule: Hold tactical expansion if player avoids backhand or uses only a floating defensive reply.

teaching_sequence: consistent first or second serve shape
hit plus-one to safe pattern target
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can make 7 of 10 second serves and execute a planned plus-one target after a controlled return.
technical_models.assessment: Serve-location plus-one task with serve-in, recovery, and next-ball target scoring.
technical_models.hold_rule: Cap serve volume and keep targets large if shoulder, elbow, back, or toss instability appears.

technical_models.skill_gate: Player returns 6 of 10 makeable serves deep or neutral and wins or neutralizes the next rally ball.
technical_models.assessment: Return-game simulation with return-in, depth, recovery, and plus-one outcome.
technical_models.hold_rule: Do not assign aggressive return patterns if neutral return percentage is below the gate.

technical_models.model: Split-step and recovery model by level
teaching_sequence: beginner: balanced ready position after hit
orange: timed split before opponent contact
green: recover to likely court position
advanced: recover by opponent, surface, and score pattern
technical_models.skill_gate: Player is balanced at opponent contact on most balls during live rally tasks.
technical_models.assessment: Coach codes ready-at-contact percentage during a 20-ball rally or point-play task.
technical_models.hold_rule: Hold new tactical complexity if recovery is late enough to make every next shot defensive.

teaching_sequence: move through the approach without overhitting
volley to open court or behind opponent
technical_models.skill_gate: Player approaches on a short ball, lands balanced, and completes the first volley or overhead decision.
technical_models.assessment: Approach-volley-point task with approach depth, net position, and first-volley decision scoring.
technical_models.hold_rule: Keep transition tasks cooperative if player cannot control approach depth or stop at net.

technical_models.skill_gate: Player can vary serve location or shape without sacrificing second-serve reliability or next-day shoulder, elbow, or back response.
technical_models.assessment: Serve chart by location, speed or intent band, second-serve percentage, plus-one outcome, and next-day symptom report.
technical_models.hold_rule: Stop adding speed or kick volume if mechanics degrade, pain rises, or serve-in rate drops below planned threshold.

technical_models.model: Advanced forehand weapon and protection model
teaching_sequence: use height, spin, and pace variation
technical_models.skill_gate: Player creates advantage with forehand patterns while unforced-error rate stays inside match-plan limits.
technical_models.assessment: Pattern charting: neutral, advantage, forced-error, winner, and unforced-error outcomes.
technical_models.hold_rule: Do not expand direction options if player leaks errors on neutral forehands.

teaching_sequence: use slice to change height or defend
attack short second serves or short balls
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can prevent opponent from repeatedly breaking down the backhand side across scored points.
technical_models.assessment: Opponent-targeted backhand drill with error count, neutralization rate, and successful direction changes.
technical_models.hold_rule: Keep advanced redirect work limited if ball recognition or spacing fails under speed.

teaching_sequence: set court position by server profile
block, drive, chip, or attack by serve quality
choose return target by score and opponent
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can select return type and court position based on serve quality while maintaining target discipline.
technical_models.assessment: Return chart by serve side, serve type, return type, target, depth, and point outcome.
technical_models.hold_rule: Simplify to neutral deep returns if aggressive return errors decide too many points.

teaching_sequence: select high-trust serve or return pattern
technical_models.skill_gate: Player executes pre-selected patterns on break point, game point, and tiebreak simulations without abandoning margin.
technical_models.assessment: Pressure-game chart for decision, execution, recovery, and emotional reset.
technical_models.hold_rule: Delay new tactical experiments in competition week if pressure execution is unstable.

teaching_sequence: recover to one-up-one-back or two-up shape
technical_models.skill_gate: Player can start and play doubles points with safe spacing, basic communication, and no repeated collision risk.
technical_models.assessment: Short doubles games scored for serve-return start, net readiness, middle call, and recovery shape.
technical_models.hold_rule: Keep formations simple if players cannot identify responsibility or recover after the first shot.

tactical_rules.rule: At red stage, teach find space and recover before teaching named patterns.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Use visible target zones and small-sided games so players experience open court, opponent position, and recovery.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player can send the ball away from opponent or into a target while returning to ready position.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player watches the shot instead of recovering or does not notice opponent location.

tactical_rules.rule: At orange stage, teach moving the opponent with crosscourt and open-court targets.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Players learn that direction changes should come from balance and time, not panic.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player can play 3-5 shot point patterns with intended direction and recovery.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player changes direction from late contact and increases error rate sharply.

tactical_rules.rule: At green stage, teach point construction: neutral, attack, defend, and transition.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Players classify incoming balls and choose neutral depth, attacking short ball, defensive height, or transition to net.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player can explain and execute the correct response to short, deep, wide, and high balls during point play.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player treats every ball as the same shot or attacks from defensive positions.

tactical_rules.rule: Absolute beginners should use large targets and net clearance before narrow targets.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Middle or crosscourt targets reduce errors and create rallies, which gives more feedback than low-margin lines.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player sustains rallies and can later shrink target size without losing form.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player aims for lines, misses early, and gets too few live-ball repetitions.

tactical_rules.rule: Intermediate baseline tactics should start with crosscourt tolerance.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Crosscourt rallies provide net margin, court length, and recovery time while building repeatable neutral patterns.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player can sustain crosscourt patterns and choose a change only from a balanced ball.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player cannot complete neutral exchanges before trying winners.

tactical_rules.rule: Changing direction down the line requires balance, spacing, and enough ball quality.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Teach down-the-line changes after crosscourt control; use clear green-light balls.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player changes direction with stable body position and recovers to cover the open court.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Direction changes create immediate errors or leave the court open without recovery.

tactical_rules.rule: Attack short balls through approach quality, not only swing speed.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Players learn to move forward, control depth, choose target, and take net position.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player converts short balls into advantage without repeated net or long errors.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player overhits short balls or stops in no-man's land after contact.

tactical_rules.rule: Defensive balls should buy time with height, depth, and recovery.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Wide or pressured balls are not attack moments; teach high crosscourt reset or deep middle reset.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player neutralizes pressure and regains court position.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player tries low-margin winners from stretched positions.

tactical_rules.rule: Advanced players should own serve-location plus-one packages.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Pair serve placement with expected return and next-ball target; chart outcomes instead of only serve percentage.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player can execute at least two reliable patterns per service box and adapt if opponent changes return position.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Serve targets are disconnected from recovery and plus-one decisions.

tactical_rules.rule: Advanced return tactics should include neutralize, pressure, and attack options.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Return choice depends on serve quality, score, server pattern, and player's strengths.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player changes return position or type for tactical reasons and controls the next ball.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Aggressive return intent lowers in-court percentage without strategic payoff.

tactical_rules.rule: Competition entry should progress from cooperative games to short match formats to standard scoring.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Use low-stakes formats first: team games, round robins, short sets, timed matches, and modified scoring.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player can score, serve in turn, manage basic etiquette, and recover emotionally between points.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player loses scoring track, avoids competition, or has large behavior swings from normal errors.

tactical_rules.rule: Advanced tactical blocks should begin from opponent and surface constraints.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Define how to start points, what to do under pressure, which patterns protect weaknesses, and how surface changes bounce and recovery.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Player enters matches with 2-3 primary patterns, adjustment triggers, and post-match chart review.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Player adds new tactics without enough practice volume or ignores tournament-week load.

tactical_rules.rule: Beginner and intermediate doubles should prioritize serve-return start, net readiness, and communication.
tactical_rules.teaching_focus: Before advanced formations, players need crosscourt returns, first volley readiness, middle-ball calls, and safe spacing.
tactical_rules.promotion_signal: Pair can start points, call middle balls, and maintain one-up-one-back or two-up shape.
tactical_rules.hold_signal: Players both chase the same ball, leave the middle open, or lose track of court roles.

physical_demands.why_it_matters: Safe stopping, turning, reaching, and recovery create more successful contacts and reduce early lower-limb overload.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Coach observes balance at contact, ability to stop after a wide ball, and recovery before opponent contact.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Do not add high-speed chase drills until the player can move, hit, and stop without falling or lunging.

physical_demands.quality: Scaled court reduces excessive reach and sprint distance.
physical_demands.why_it_matters: A court matched to the player lets movement, timing, and contact develop without constant late contact or maximal recovery runs.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Player can reach most balls with controlled steps and recover without repeated emergency lunges.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Increase court size only when rallies remain playable and movement quality does not collapse.

physical_demands.why_it_matters: Players must repeat short accelerations, decelerations, lateral recoveries, and setup steps across rallies and service games.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Track movement quality and error rate in later drill rounds or after several games.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Build conditioning with tennis-like work-rest rhythms and movement directions.

physical_demands.quality: Advanced conditioning must reflect tennis rally-rest structure.
physical_demands.why_it_matters: Tennis is intermittent; useful conditioning supports repeated explosive points plus between-point recovery, not generic fatigue alone.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Chart point duration, recovery heart-rate behavior, movement speed, and technical error drift.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Use point-based intervals, serve-return blocks, and scenario games with planned rest.

physical_demands.why_it_matters: Serve development adds repetitive shoulder, elbow, wrist, trunk, and back stress, especially when volume and intent rise together.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Track serve count, high-intent serve count, overhead count, and next-day shoulder, elbow, wrist, and back symptoms.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Add serve volume or velocity gradually and avoid combining serve spikes with heavy upper-body gym stress.

physical_demands.why_it_matters: Chronological age does not fully describe height, strength, coordination, emotional readiness, or injury tolerance.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Record recent growth, coordination changes, fatigue, soreness, and confidence when moving between stages.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Hold or regress temporarily during growth-related coordination drops or symptom spikes.

physical_demands.why_it_matters: Adult beginners may have strength, stiffness, prior injuries, low aerobic base, or limited deceleration capacity despite understanding instructions quickly.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Screen for prior pain, ability to stop and change direction, tolerance to serving, and recovery after first sessions.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Progress ball speed and court coverage by physical response, not only technical comprehension.

physical_demands.quality: Tournament and competition density changes training readiness.
physical_demands.why_it_matters: Multiple matches compress serve volume, deceleration load, emotional stress, and recovery windows.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Track matches per week, match duration, high-intent serves, soreness, sleep, and next-practice quality.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Reduce new technical load and heavy conditioning during dense competition periods.

physical_demands.quality: Court surface modifies movement and load.
physical_demands.why_it_matters: Hard court impact, clay sliding and longer exchanges, and grass-like low bounce environments change timing, stopping, and tactical choices.
physical_demands.assessment_or_observation: Record surface, movement errors, slipping, stopping quality, point length, and soreness response.
physical_demands.progression_rule: Do not treat all full-court training loads as equivalent across surfaces.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: Full-speed yellow ball before the player controls full-court depth, contact height, and recovery.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Return to green or mixed green-yellow tasks if rally quality collapses or movement becomes unsafe.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: Rapid increase in serves, kick serves, high-intent first serves, or serve plus overhead drills.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Cap serve volume, reduce intent, and emphasize rhythm and mechanics until next-day shoulder, elbow, wrist, and back response is stable.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: Late contact, grip squeezing, mishits, heavy topspin volume, large racket changes, or high serve volume.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Reduce ball speed, shorten sessions, check grip and contact point, and avoid high-volume spin or serve work until symptoms settle.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Shoulder overload from serving and overheads
injury_or_load_risks.trigger: Repeated overhead actions without scapular control, trunk contribution, or recovery time.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Lower overhead count and separate technical serving from maximal serving when soreness appears.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Lumbar spine irritation from rotation and serve arching
injury_or_load_risks.trigger: High serve load, aggressive trunk extension, repeated open-stance rotation, fatigue-compromised mechanics, or poor hip/trunk control.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Reduce serve and high-rotation volume, rebuild trunk and hip control, and avoid maximal intent until pain response is stable.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Knee, ankle, calf, or Achilles overload from stopping and changing direction
injury_or_load_risks.trigger: Large court coverage, hard-court impact, repeated wide-ball recoveries, fatigue, or poor deceleration mechanics.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Reduce chase-drill density, use smaller court tasks, and rebuild stopping mechanics before adding speed.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: Rapid height change followed by late contact, balance loss, soreness, or sudden confidence drop.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Temporarily reduce court size, ball speed, and competition pressure while rebuilding movement and timing.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: High tennis-only volume, limited free play, ranking pressure, or frequent tournaments before broad athletic foundation.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Protect multi-sport or broad movement exposure and use competition as learning, not only selection.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: New player starts several sessions per week, full yellow-ball rallies, or prolonged serving before tissues adapt.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Use shorter sessions, slower balls, lower serve counts, and gradual full-court exposure.

injury_or_load_risks.trigger: New technique, new tactics, or new conditioning load introduced near important match play.
injury_or_load_risks.hold_or_regress_rule: Keep competition week to rehearsed patterns, readiness, recovery, and small tactical reminders.

training_implications.implication: Use a repeatable lesson template for all levels.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Warm-up and athletic readiness, skill reminder, live-ball technical task, decision game, scored application, quick assessment, pain or fatigue check.
training_implications.assessment: Lesson record captures task scores and readiness notes.

training_implications.implication: Adult beginner courses should be sequenced toward playing real points quickly.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: A six-session block can progress from groundstroke rallying to forward movement and volleys, recovery and positioning, serve and return, doubles teamwork, and a final play event.
training_implications.assessment: Course completion requires serve-rally-score independence, basic scoring, and comfort entering a social play format.

training_implications.implication: Red-stage blocks should be game-led and high-success.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Use small-court rally games, target zones, simple serves, partner cooperation, and frequent play starts.
training_implications.assessment: Rally count, correct court position, basic scorekeeping, and safe movement.

training_implications.implication: Orange-stage blocks should add depth, direction, and recovery.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Use half-to-three-quarter court rallies, crosscourt games, serve direction, return readiness, and short-ball decisions.
training_implications.assessment: Depth target success, crosscourt rally tolerance, serve-in rate, and recovery readiness.

training_implications.implication: Green-stage blocks should prepare full-court yellow transition without rushing it.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Use full-court green-ball rallies, serve-return games, depth and height control, transition decisions, and short-set competition.
training_implications.assessment: Full-court rally, serve-return start, movement quality, and post-session symptom stability.

training_implications.implication: Yellow-ball entry should use mixed exposure before full replacement when needed.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Blend green and yellow tasks: green for learning new control tasks, yellow for assessed full-court points and competition preparation.
training_implications.assessment: No drop in rally quality, contact spacing, recovery, or pain response across yellow sessions.

training_implications.implication: Beginner promotion should require rally, serve, return, movement, and scoring gates.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Before moving up a ball or court stage, require repeatable cooperative rally success, legal point starts, return-in competence, balanced recovery, basic scoring, and no pain spike.
training_implications.assessment: Composite promotion assessment with pass, hold, or mixed-stage recommendation.

training_implications.implication: Hold rules should be explicit and visible to coaches.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Hold progression if two or more key gates fail repeatedly, if pain rises, if confidence drops sharply, or if a new ball stage reduces rally learning volume.
training_implications.assessment: Hold reason is selected from contact, movement, tactical, scoring, confidence, behavior, or load response.

training_implications.implication: Intermediate weekly training should connect technique to match patterns.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: A useful week includes one pattern session, one serve-return session, one movement or conditioning exposure, and one scored-play assessment when frequency allows.
training_implications.assessment: Track pattern success, serve and return reliability, movement quality under fatigue, and match decision notes.

training_implications.implication: Advanced blocks should start with a match problem.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Choose the block goal from charted needs: serve plus-one, return games, backhand tolerance, forehand finishing, net transition, surface adaptation, or pressure scoring.
training_implications.assessment: Use match chart outcomes before and after the block.

training_implications.implication: Assess frequently but keep beginner tests short.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Use quick 10-ball or 20-ball tasks inside normal lessons so players are assessed in context rather than through long testing sessions.
training_implications.assessment: Store attempt date, ball stage, court size, feed type, live or cooperative setting, and result.

training_implications.implication: Create a competition ladder that scales pressure gradually.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Order formats as cooperative games, team challenges, round robin short games, short sets, standard matches, tournament weekends, and multi-match events.
training_implications.assessment: Promotion depends on scoring accuracy, serve-start reliability, behavior, recovery, and post-event load response.

training_implications.implication: New skills need lower volume than mastered skills.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Limit repetitions when teaching new serve, high-spin forehand, slice, overhead, or full-court movement tasks; expand volume only after mechanics and symptoms are stable.
training_implications.assessment: Track new-skill volume separately from total session duration.

training_implications.implication: Youth progression records should explain why a child is held, promoted, or mixed-stage.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Report the next development target in simple categories: rally, serve, return, movement, tactics, scoring, confidence, or load.
training_implications.assessment: Parent-facing summary should avoid ranking labels and focus on developmental readiness.

training_implications.implication: Temporary regression to a slower ball is valid for learning.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Use a slower ball or smaller court to learn a new skill, rebuild confidence, protect load, or restore tactical success before returning to normal match conditions.
training_implications.assessment: Record regression reason and planned retest date.

training_implications.implication: Do not prescribe advanced tactics before ball control supports them.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: If rally tolerance, serve-in rate, or directional control are below gate, the plan should assign control-based games rather than detailed opponent exploitation.
training_implications.assessment: Tactical progression locked until minimum control metrics pass.

training_implications.implication: Advanced competition-week training should reduce novelty.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Rehearse known patterns, manage serve count, sharpen return decisions, and maintain movement readiness rather than rebuilding technique.
training_implications.assessment: Monitor readiness, soreness, and serve quality rather than chasing training volume.

training_implications.implication: Every generated lesson should preserve the evidence basis of its level rules.
training_implications.lesson_or_block_application: Attach source IDs to progression, assessment, safety, and competition recommendations.
training_implications.assessment: Backend can audit whether a lesson is unsupported, official-framework-based, or peer-review-informed.

backend_records_to_create.purpose: Define beginner tennis as serve-rally-score competence with basic contact, movement, scoring, and low pain response.
Define intermediate tennis as reliable serve, return, rally tolerance, direction control, movement recovery, and simple pattern execution.
Define advanced tennis as context-specific performance: serve-return-plus-one packages, opponent plans, surface adaptation, pressure execution, and load control.
Store red ball, small court, lower bounce/speed, and target beginner/youth outcomes.
Store orange ball bridge rules for larger court, increased movement, depth, direction, serve, and return development.
Store green ball full-court transition rules before regular yellow-ball competition.
Store yellow ball readiness rules for full-speed tennis, intermediate-to-advanced training, and standard competition formats.
Assess readiness to move between red, orange, green, and yellow stages.
Promote only when technical, tactical, physical, scoring, confidence, and load-response gates are acceptable.
Hold or temporarily regress if a new stage lowers rally volume, movement quality, confidence, or pain response.
Generate level-scaled lessons using warm-up, skill, decision, play, assessment, and recovery-check blocks.
Provide a six-session adult beginner sequence using slower balls and rapid entry into serve-rally-score play.
Store youth readiness beyond tennis strokes: physical literacy, confidence, character, connection, creativity, maturity, and competition response.
Store forehand, backhand, serve, return, volley, overhead, and slice teaching progressions by level and ball stage.
Store split-step, first step, adjustment steps, recovery, approach movement, and deceleration progressions.
Store tactical concepts from find-space to crosscourt tolerance, serve plus-one, return plus-one, score-state plans, and opponent-specific plans.
Progress players from cooperative games to low-stakes events, short formats, standard matches, and tournament-density preparation.
Control serve and overhead progression by count, intent, mechanics, and next-day symptom response.
Control movement and impact exposure when players move to larger courts or faster balls.
Record every progression assessment so level movement is auditable.
Map each lesson, gate, safety rule, and backend progression record to official or peer-reviewed evidence.
